title: The Definition of Psychological Safety
author: Tom Geraghty
summary: Tom Geraghty explains why his team opens every talk and workshop by restating the working definition of psychological safety: the belief, in a group, that it is safe to take interpersonal risks. He argues that a shared definition lets people converge on decisions, anchors cumulative research, and guards against epistemic drift, citing how Agile and DevOps lost precision. Definitions also set boundaries, so psychological safety covers interpersonal risk and not physical, business or health risk. He warns against definitions that are too thin, such as simply speaking up without fear, and too broad, such as comfort, no accountability or being your authentic self. Definitions should still evolve, but through community consensus and transparent records. He treats clear terms as a matter of intellectual integrity and as protection against the concept becoming a meaningless leadership fad.
points: Psychological safety is the belief that interpersonal risks such as speaking up with ideas, questions, concerns and mistakes will not bring negative social or professional consequences.
Shared definitions prevent conversations and debates from failing simply because participants use the same term differently.
Terms suffer epistemic drift when they stretch to cover too much, as Agile and DevOps did, which weakens their usefulness.
Definitions that equate psychological safety with comfort, no accountability or being your authentic self misrepresent it.
Definitions can legitimately evolve, but through community consensus and documented change, not individual or commercial reinterpretation.
quotes: Psychological safety is defined asthe belief, in a group, that we are safe to take interpersonal risks. It’s the belief that we are able to speak up with ideas, questions, concerns and mistakes, and that we won’t suffer negative social or professional consequences as a result.
A clear definition acts like a compass pointing to True North, without which we could be heading in different directions.
Terms often suffer from “epistemic drift” – a passive drift away from their intended meaning.

Psychological safety, for example, addresses only interpersonal risks, not physical, business, health or other risks. When psychological safety is mistakenly framed as permitting business or safety risks, it misleads people.

Overly simplistic definitions, like “Psychological safety is the ability to speak up without fear,” reduce the concept to just “speaking up” and overlook the complexities of social interactions and the need to create an environment where people can communicate and share in different ways.

Conversely, overly broad definitions may suggest psychological safety is about always feeling comfortable, having no accountability, or being your “authentic self”. These frame psychological safety as synonymous with comfort – which it is absolutely not.
Our shared commitment to rigour, clarity, and continual learning and growth in this area is what will help keep psychological safety from drifting into just another meaningless leadership fad.
